skill.name: rust-async-patterns
skill.description: Guides Rust developers through async programming patterns with Tokio, including tasks, channels, streams, cancellation, error handling, and debugging.
skill.summary: Learn practical Tokio patterns for reliable async Rust services.
skill.author: sickn33

security_audit.summary: All static findings were adjudicated as false positives. The flagged Tokio spawn calls, URL, SQL, tracing, and backtick references are Markdown examples or file references, not executable marketplace behavior. No prompt injection or malicious intent was found in the cited files.

sqlx::query!("DELETE FROM entities WHERE id = $1", id)

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 87 is a Tokio JoinSet task example inside Markdown documentation. It spawns an async Rust future, not an external process or shell command.
Line 137 is a Tokio producer task in a channel example. The code is documentation-only and does not invoke an operating system command.
Line 165 is a Tokio oneshot channel example. It sends a string through an async task and does not execute a process.
Line 176 is a Tokio watch channel example in a fenced Markdown block. It demonstrates async task scheduling, not command execution.
Line 257 is a graceful shutdown example using tokio::spawn with a cancellation token. It does not run shell commands or process user input.
Line 287 is a broadcast shutdown example using tokio::spawn. It is a Rust concurrency pattern, not an external command launcher.
Line 464 is a resource-management example that returns a connection to a pool with tokio::spawn. It is not a process-spawn API and appears only in documentation.
Line 491 instruments a spawned Tokio task with a tracing span. It schedules an async future and does not execute external programs.
Line 210 defines process_request and calls a placeholder fetch_data helper. The cited line does not create an HTTP client or send data to a network endpoint.
Line 61 uses https://api.example.com in a quick-start code example. The helper is simulated and the URL is documentation placeholder text, not live exfiltration behavior.
Line 322 is a parameterized sqlx SELECT example for repository access. It is normal application data access documentation, not host reconnaissance.
Line 341 is a parameterized sqlx DELETE example. It targets an example entities table and does not inspect the local system.
Line 490 creates a tracing span named worker. It is observability instrumentation and does not collect system inventory or secrets.
Line 29 uses Markdown backticks around a resource path. It is an instruction to open a documentation file, not Ruby or shell execution.
Line 33 uses Markdown backticks around the same resource path. It is a safe file reference in prose and contains no executable code.
Line 1 is a normal Markdown heading: Rust Async Patterns Implementation Playbook. No obfuscated JavaScript or bracket-chain payload is present there.

content.value_statement: Async Rust code can be hard to structure safely and clearly. This skill gives practical Tokio patterns for tasks, channels, shutdown, errors, and debugging.
actual_capabilities: Explains core Rust async concepts such as futures, tasks, runtimes, and await points.
Provides Tokio quick-start dependencies and a minimal async application pattern.
Shows concurrent task execution with JoinSet and bounded stream buffering.
Demonstrates mpsc, broadcast, oneshot, and watch channel patterns.
Covers graceful shutdown with cancellation tokens and broadcast signals.
Includes examples for async traits, streams, resource pools, and tracing.
limitations: It is a documentation skill and does not execute or test Rust code.
Examples use placeholder functions and must be adapted to real services.
The guidance focuses on Tokio rather than every Rust async runtime.
It does not replace production security, load, or correctness reviews.

use_cases.title: Design a Tokio Service
use_cases.description: Plan task structure, channels, cancellation, and tracing for a new async backend service.

use_cases.title: Refactor Concurrent Workflows
use_cases.description: Replace blocking or unbounded async code with bounded task and stream patterns.

use_cases.title: Review Team Async Code
use_cases.description: Check existing Rust code for common async mistakes, missing cancellation, and weak observability.

prompt_templates.title: Explain Async Basics
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain how Rust futures, await points, tasks, and the Tokio runtime work together. Use a small service example.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a Tokio Service
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me design an async Rust service with bounded concurrency, channels, graceful shutdown, error handling, and tracing.

prompt_templates.title: Review My Async Code
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my async Rust design for blocking calls, unbounded spawns, lock usage across await points, and cancellation gaps.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Concurrent Pipeline
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a production Tokio pipeline with backpressure, worker coordination, retries, shutdown, resource pooling, and runtime debugging hooks.

output_examples.input: Review an async worker pool design for reliability.
output: A short risk summary covering unbounded tasks, missing cancellation, and error propagation.
A revised design using bounded channels, JoinSet, and tracing spans.
A verification checklist for shutdown, backpressure, and failure handling.

output_examples.input: Plan graceful shutdown for a Tokio service.
output: A shutdown flow using cancellation tokens and signal handling.
Recommendations for task cleanup, timeout limits, and final logging.
A list of edge cases to test before deployment.

output_examples.input: Explain when to use Rust async channels.
output_examples.output: A comparison of mpsc, broadcast, oneshot, and watch channels with recommended use cases for each pattern.

best_practices: Use bounded concurrency for network, disk, and worker tasks.
Plan cancellation and shutdown behavior before adding more tasks.
Add tracing spans around important async boundaries.
anti_patterns: Spawning unlimited tasks without backpressure or limits.
Holding locks across await points in shared state code.
Ignoring task errors or dropping join handles silently.

faq.question: Does this skill execute Rust code?
faq.answer: No. It provides guidance and examples for async Rust design and review.

faq.question: Which runtime does it focus on?
faq.answer: It focuses on Tokio and common ecosystem crates such as futures, async-trait, anyhow, and tracing.

faq.question: Can it help debug slow async services?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers tracing, task instrumentation, cancellation, and common performance mistakes.

faq.question: Is it useful for beginners?
faq.answer: Yes. It starts with core concepts and then moves into practical patterns.

faq.question: Can Claude, Codex, or Claude Code use it?
faq.answer: Yes. The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: Does it cover database access?
faq.answer: It includes repository examples with async traits and parameterized sqlx queries.
